books.section: Topic 4.3 Politics and Regional Interests, B. The American System and Sectionalism
Henry Clay and the American System

stimulus.text:
| Part of the plan | What it would do |
|---|---|---|
| Protective tariff | Tax imported goods so American-made goods cost less |
| Second Bank of the United States | Steady the currency and lend credit for business |
| Internal improvements | Build roads and canals to link the regions |

Henry Clay of Kentucky called the three parts his American System. Congress chartered the Second Bank and passed a protective tariff in 1816.

stem: The “internal improvements” part of the American System faced its hardest obstacle in the fact that

options.text: no American knew how to build a canal anywhere before 1825
options.misconception: New York built the Erie Canal between 1817 and 1825; the skill existed before the canal opened.

options.text: Congress refused to charter the Second Bank of the United States
options.misconception: Congress chartered the Second Bank in 1816; the Bank was the easy part of the plan.

options.text: Henry Clay opposed all federal spending on transportation
options.misconception: Clay championed internal improvements; opposing them would undo his own plan.

options.text: presidents doubted the Constitution allowed federal building, so states built the canals

rationales.A: Americans did know how to build canals. New York dug the Erie Canal from 1817 to 1825, before this question’s period ends.
rationales.B: The Bank was chartered in 1816, the same year as the first protective tariff. The Bank was not the obstacle.
rationales.C: Clay proposed internal improvements himself. He is the plan’s champion, not its opponent.
rationales.D: Madison vetoed the Bonus Bill for internal improvements in 1817 on constitutional grounds, and Monroe shared the doubt. So the great canal of the age was built by New York State, not by Congress.
rationales.general:
1. Ask which part of the plan lagged. The tariff and the Bank both arrived in 1816; federal roads and canals did not.
2. Ask why. Presidents doubted the Constitution gave Congress power to build them.
3. Check the evidence. Madison vetoed the Bonus Bill in 1817, while New York went ahead and built the Erie Canal itself.
4. Put it together. The obstacle was constitutional doubt, and the states filled the gap.
Background: Madison’s 1817 veto of the Bonus Bill and Monroe’s doubts kept federal internal improvements small, while states took the lead.
Remember: when a plan stalls, ask which power is in doubt, not just which money is short.
